item.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
item.description: The DOJ's embrace of fair use for AI training breaks with the White House's own framework, as OpenAI, Microsoft and news groups battle over copyright.
item.content:encoded:
One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

item.title: Darius Rucker says he used to drink a bottle of whiskey a day during wild Hootie & the Blowfish years
item.description: Darius Rucker admits drinking a bottle of whiskey a day on the road as Hootie & the Blowfish fame fueled substance abuse in new Hulu documentary.
item.content:encoded:
Darius Rucker's meteoric rise to fame as the lead singer of Hootie & The Blowfish was captured in the latest Hulu documentary, "They Called Me Hootie."

Breaking onto the scene in the early '90s, the group of college friends from South Carolina broke records with "Cracked Rear View" released in 1994, but fame and fortune came at a cost and Rucker soon spiraled into substance abuse and drinking issues at the peak of the band's popularity.

Rucker, 60, admitted that at one point he was drinking one bottle of whiskey per day while on the road, and casual drug use became routine.

BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG

"I smoked a little pot," Rucker said. "If we had a day over, someone would get some acid." After the band upgraded to a tour bus, things took a drastic detour.

"One day, I came back to our bus, I walked in the back and two of the guys were lining up some cocaine," Rucker said. "And the party just was on from that point."

‘BACK TO THE FUTURE’ STAR CHRISTOPHER LLOYD CONFESSES HE WAS ‘HOOKED’ ON COCAINE DURING ‘TAXI’ YEARS

He added, "We earned our reputation. We went crazy, man. It was rock and roll."

Rucker recalled once buying trash bags full of mushrooms from someone on the bus.

"I'm like, 'Mushrooms? Really? How many mushrooms you got?' 'We've got two garbage bags of mushrooms,'" he said. "And he's like, 'Well, we're probably gonna make about $45,000.' It’s like, 'What if we give you [$30,000] right now?'

"I went and got T-shirt money and came back with two garbage bags that we kept in our freezers for two and a half years. I always said we never had a drug problem because we could always afford it."

Rucker became "instant friends" with Woody Harrelson after meeting backstage following a show, and the pair soon became smoking buddies. Harrelson guessed they had "maybe smoked about 100,000 joints together."

"What do you do when you smoke joints? You just sit and talk. I just loved listening to him spin a yarn," Harrelson said.

COUNTRY SINGER RUSTON KELLY COMMITS TO SOBRIETY AFTER RELAPSING ON DRUGS FOLLOWING FREAK GOLF CART CRASH

At one point, bandmate Mark Bryan remembered when Rucker's penchant for rock 'n' roll impacted the band after he took ecstasy before a gig in London.

"He decided to, like, start exploring the theater during the show," Bryan said. "It felt to me like we were losing the crowd, which is the worst feeling at any time at any show. He probably didn’t feel that way. He probably thought he was taking things to the next level. "

Rucker admitted a girl at the show gave him the drugs, but didn't know why he took it, and said he "could've waited till the show was over, but, you know, I just took it."

"We went on the stage and I was introducing songs we weren’t playing," Rucker said before Bryan explained they had a "huge fight" backstage.

"I headbutted a cinderblock wall," he said. "I’ll never forget doing that. We were not on the same page in that moment."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

While Rucker's life on the road was bumpy, his wife back home was having an equally difficult time with Rucker's touring habits.

"She said that I could straighten up and we would be happy, or I could keep living that life and she'll figure out how she can make me miserable," Rucker recalled.

"The day before she said that was the last day I partied like that. The next day I called and said I need my own bus."

While taking a break from the band, Rucker visited Harrelson's Hawaiian home, where the singer had the "two best weeks" of his life before tragedy nearly struck.

"We had a blast. We did naked yoga, and I ate so pure and vegan," Rucker remembered.

While walking on the cliffs one day, Harrelson asked if Rucker could swim, and told him if he jumped in, he'd have to navigate a strong rip current.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"I dive out, and I open my eyes and look both ways, and I realize, there's no beach and all I see is fish," Rucker said. "And I come up and I start to swim out and I'm caught."

Harrelson admitted the water was "a little rugged that day and he probably shouldn't have gone in."

"It seemed like forever that we were out there trying to get out," Rucker remembered. "I had gotten myself to a peace. I had accepted that God had given me this amazing life that is exactly what I asked for, and if it had to end right there, then when I got to heaven I was going to say thank you."

"He looked at me, and it was just like Woody from 'Cheers,' he looked at me and giggled and said ‘not on my watch.’"

"I wasn't going to let that happen," Harrelson said before Rucker chimed in that it was "surreal. Woody Harrelson had really literally just saved my life."

The band celebrated the 30th anniversary of their massively successful album "Cracked Rear View" in 2024.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

With tracks including "Only Wanna Be With You," "Hold My Hand" and "Let Her Cry," the debut catalog for the band from South Carolina was released in July 1994 and has been certified platinum 21 times over.

Hootie & the Blowfish went on to release four more studio albums before going on hiatus in 2008, leading Rucker to pursue an entirely different genre: country music.

In 2023, Rucker released his eighth solo album, "Carolyn's Boy," a tribute to his late mother who died in 1992 just as Hootie was picking up steam.

Rucker noted that his biggest disappointment was that his mother never got a chance to see his success.

"At first it was really hard to accept, I mean it was so out of the blue," he said of his mother's death.

"To know that she didn't get to see me do what I told her I was going to do since I was five-years-old. She never got to sit on the phone talking to her girlfriends about me being on David Letterman tonight and how she was going to stay up even though she had to work early tomorrow ... and how she never got to do that is still heartbreaking."

item.title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Resurfaced video appears to show NYC mayor arrested by NYPD group he is disbanding
item.description: Resurfaced video shows Zohran Mamdani being detained by the NYPD Special Response Group, the same unit he later ordered dismantled as mayor.
item.content:encoded:
Years before New York City's socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani ordered the dismantling of a specialized police task force, he'd been detained by its members, resurfaced video the mayor himself tweeted in 2021 appears to show.

The video appears to show the arresting officer's vest reading "NYPD Special Response Group" across the back during a protest against an end to the city's COVID-era moratorium on evictions.

The mayor's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

MICHAEL RUIZ: NEW YORK'S GUTTED POLICE UNIT WAS MORE THAN A PROTEST SQUAD

Mamdani announced that the group will be dissolved at a news briefing early Monday. He had campaigned on the issue in part due to the unit's role in responding to organized protests — and riots — including those that exploded after George Floyd's death in 2020, demonstrations against Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Israel's war with Palestinian Hamas terrorists.

The images were recirculated earlier this week by Crain's New York, a local outlet focused on business, politics and real estate.

A second video, recorded by the local ABC affiliate, appears to show Mamdani arrested again by the unit shortly before he announced his mayoral bid in 2024.

On Monday, Mamdani said he would disband the group and divvy up its responsibilities — which included crowd control at protests and riots, critical incident response and counterterrorism — between three new entities and the NYPD's Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau.

One of the new units is the unarmed Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD). This civilian team won't have arrest authority.

"His voters won’t care," said Joseph Giacalone, a retired NYPD sergeant and criminal justice professor. "These transplants are all renters using mommy and daddy’s money to live in NYC, and when things go south, and they will, they’ll flee back home."

Upcoming events like the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade and New Year's ball drop will not be impacted since the changes aren't slated to go into effect until spring 2027.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said in a statement that the restructuring would not "diminish the NYPD’s ability to protect New Yorkers, or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat."

item.title: Suspect in alleged rape of LSU student killed by car fights to keep mom’s warning texts out of December trial
item.description: Desmond Carter's texts about his mother's advice to stay silent are central to a court fight in the alleged rape of a Louisiana State University student.
item.content:encoded:
As a man in Louisiana prepares to stand trial next month for the alleged rape of a Louisiana State University student who was later struck and killed by a car, text messages show he sent a series of frantic text messages about his mother's instructions to stay quiet, according to court documents.

Madison Brooks, a 19-year-old LSU student at the time, was allegedly gang-raped by a group of men after a night out at a bar near the Baton Rouge campus in 2023, then struck and killed by a car. Her blood alcohol concentration was 0.319% at the time of her death, nearly four times Louisiana's legal driving limit for adults 21 and older.

Desmond Carter, 21, one of several men charged in connection with Brooks' alleged rape, exchanged a series of text messages with co-defendants Casen Carver, Kaivon Washington and Everett Lee, repeatedly saying that his mother had warned him not to speak with police.

SLAIN LSU STUDENT MADISON BROOKS’ ALLEGED RAPIST WANTS SUPPORTERS BANNED FROM WEARING PINK AT TRIAL: REPORT

MADISON BROOKS RAPE SUSPECT'S ATTORNEY HELD IN CONTEMPT FOR USING HER NAME TO TRY TO BAN PINK IN COURTROOM

The messages were exchanged after the alleged gang rape, and Carter's defense attorney sought to prevent them from being introduced as evidence at trial. In a court filing submitted in September, his attorney contended that admitting the text messages as trial evidence would infringe on his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.

Judge Gail Horne Ray has yet to issue a ruling. The court document doesn't differentiate who each text message was sent to.

Carter has pleaded not guilty to charges of first- and third-degree rape, with his trial scheduled to begin Dec. 7. Both Carter and Washington maintain that their sexual encounters with Brooks were consensual.

Prosecutors allege that Carver drove the vehicle where Brooks was allegedly raped and recorded the encounter. He has pleaded not guilty to charges of principal to rape and video voyeurism.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

The men told police that Brooks asked to be taken home after the incident, providing multiple incorrect addresses before requesting to be let out near a subdivision, where they said she wandered into the street and was struck by a car.

The driver of the car that hit her remained on the scene and was ultimately cleared of charges.

"Maddie felt safe that night, she thought these were her friends and I think a lot of selfish choices were made that night, and ultimately it led to a horrific ending," Brooks' mother, Ashley Baustert, previously told Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital has reached out to attorneys for all men.

Forty years after their toddler vanished, a Southern California family is living a bizarre nightmare: a woman allegedly staking out their home claims to be their missing daughter, but refuses a basic ancestry DNA test unless it's a court-admissible lab procedure.

According to a recent report by the Los Angeles Times, the woman, legally named Cindy Rae Enders, won’t leave 83-year-old Mike Bradbury and his surviving daughter, Emily, alone. The elderly father is now largely confined to his bed, making the ongoing harassment even more distressing for the vulnerable household.

Enders has tattooed the missing girl’s name and 1981 birth year into her skin and regularly circles the family's Twentynine Palms property in a vehicle sporting the vanity plate "LANNB."

She also leaves behind disturbing mementos, dropping off strange figurines and mailing photographs of Mike's late wife, Patty, with captions calling her "mom."

Keith Hank, Emily’s partner, told the Times that Enders will frequently idle her car outside their residence for extended periods, whistling and blasting music for up to an hour.

But because her behavior hasn't crossed the line into physical violence, local deputies have told the family their hands are tied. Hank has called the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department multiple times, only to be told by dispatchers that without an explicit threat, law enforcement cannot forcibly intervene.

The nightmare stems from an October 1984 camping trip in Joshua Tree, where the family had gone for a weekend to escape their cramped Huntington Beach condominium.

During the trip, 3-year-old Laura Ann Bradbury wandered off while following her older brother to a portable restroom and ultimately disappeared without a trace.

Her desperate father poured his own funds into a private detective, background checks and personal surveillance stings, while her face famously became one of the first printed on milk cartons during a nationwide frenzy.

The family spent weeks living in a borrowed RV at the campsite and distributed millions of flyers through a dedicated nonprofit.

The first real break in the case came in 1986 when hikers stumbled upon pieces of a small skull roughly three miles from the campground. More than 100 searchers combed the desert for clothing or additional remains, yet nothing else was ever found.

Advanced genetic profiling later confirmed with near-absolute certainty that the skull belonged to Laura, the Times reported. The tragedy broke the family, with Laura's mother secretly writing agonizing letters to her missing daughter and hiding them in a sock drawer until her death from cancer in 2001.

Despite the physical evidence of Laura's death, Enders maintains she is the missing toddler. She told the Times she had a chaotic upbringing in the foster system, attending 14 different schools by the fourth grade, and insisted the man who raised her confessed on his deathbed that they were not biologically related.

The Bradburys have offered a simple resolution — a standard commercial ancestry test — but Enders has rejected it, demanding a strict, court-admissible lab procedure instead. Her own family isn't buying her story, either.

James Hunt, her stepfather, told the Times that Enders has a history of severe substance abuse and making up wild stories. Her credibility is further strained by a sprawling criminal rap sheet in Nevada, where she previously served jail time for auto theft and burglary, alongside a string of older misdemeanors including battery and child endangerment.

For the surviving Bradburys, the ongoing harassment is unbearable. Hank admits they now keep their blinds completely drawn and are constantly looking over their shoulders, with the stress recently triggering a severe episode that left Emily gasping for breath on the couch.

Emily, who battles a severe heart condition, physically holds the proof that Enders is lying. Presenting a small crematory box to the Times reporter in the harsh desert sun, Emily made it clear she knows exactly where her sibling is.

item.title: SJSU volleyball finishes near bottom of conference as Trump admin battle, coach allegations loom over program
item.description: San José State University finished ninth in the Mountain West at 9-20, after a transgender athlete scandal sparked lawsuits and federal Title IX findings.
item.content:encoded:
The San José State University's women's volleyball program continued a steep decline after its infamous trans athlete scandal, as the fallout of the scandal continues to linger for the university in multiple legal battles.

The program's 2026 season ended on Thursday with this year's team finishing near the bottom of the Mountain West Conference.

The Spartans finished ninth out of 10 teams in the conference, with a 9-20 overall record and just four conference victories. The team closed its season Thursday with a five-set loss to UNLV, missing the conference tournament for the second consecutive year.

The disappointing finish marks a sharp contrast to 2024, when SJSU reached the Mountain West championship match amid a national controversy over transgender athlete Blaire Fleming's participation on its women's team, and public resistance by female teammate Brooke Slusser.

That season triggered multiple lawsuits, federal investigations and a political conflict that has continued well beyond the departure of the athletes at the center of the original dispute. At least seven of the team's players entered the transfer portal right after the 2024 season ended, as the program has declined for two straight seasons since that controversial season.

INSIDE THE FALLOUT OF THE SJSU VOLLEYBALL SCANDAL: ‘THIS IS AN OBVIOUS PROBLEM’

In 2026, the controversy expanded. SJSU sued the Trump administration over federal Title IX findings against the university.

New allegations of misconduct surfaced against head coach Todd Kress, including an alleged physical assault involving a former player at another university nearly three decades ago. And a former assistant coach filed a new lawsuit alleging retaliation, religious discrimination and intimidation.

Despite the legal disputes and allegations, Kress remains the program's head coach and appears to still be the public face of its future. On Tuesday, Nov. 17, SJSU's athletic department announced the signing of six recruits for the 2027 season, featuring individual evaluations from Kress praising the incoming athletes and discussing their expected roles in the program.

In July, Fox News Digital first reported that a former Fairfield University volleyball player had accused Kress of physically assaulting her during a team trip in 1998.

The woman, who has remained anonymous publicly, alleged that Kress physically restrained and humiliated her in a hotel room and pressured her to consume alcohol.

She said she notified SJSU athletic director Jeff Konya in October 2024 because she was concerned about the safety of women playing under Kress, as documents show that former SJSU legal counsel Peter Lim thanked her and her attorney for meeting with him to discuss the allegations in November of that year.

On Tuesday, OutKick reported new correspondence in which SJSU Vice President for People and Culture Harly Neumann confirmed the university reviewed the woman's complaint but said it lacked authority to pursue allegations involving conduct at another institution before Kress's employment.

"The University takes all reports seriously. The University has established processes for reviewing and addressing such reports and followed those here," Neumann wrote.

"However, SJSU’s authority to investigate allegations is limited to matters that occurred within its educational programs and activities."

Neumann also acknowledged the university's responsibility to consider information relevant to the safety of current student-athletes.

The former player disputed the university's explanation, questioning whether officials evaluated her allegations alongside complaints involving Kress's conduct at SJSU.

Fairfield University also addressed the matter in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Fairfield University unequivocally condemns sexual assault, sexual violence, harassment, and all forms of sexual misconduct. Such behavior has no place at Fairfield or in any community. As a Jesuit Catholic University, we are committed to the dignity and inherent worth of every person and to fostering a community grounded in respect, care, and responsibility for one another," Fairfield said.

The university did not disclose whether it investigated the alleged 1998 incident.

The season unfolded while the university fought a separate battle over the federal government's interpretation of Title IX.

In January, the U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights concluded that SJSU violated Title IX during the 2022-2024 volleyball seasons by allowing a transgender athlete to compete on its women's team and by failing to adequately address complaints from female athletes.

The investigation began in February 2025, after President Donald Trump returned to office and issued an executive order directing federal agencies to restrict transgender participation in women's sports.

The Education Department's findings alleged that SJSU denied women equal athletic opportunities and mishandled discrimination complaints. Federal officials proposed a resolution agreement requiring changes to university policies and remedial measures for affected athletes.

SJSU and the California State University system rejected the findings, maintaining that the university followed the applicable NCAA rules and state and federal law during the seasons in question.

In March, the Education Department escalated the dispute by issuing a letter warning of potential enforcement action after SJSU declined to enter the proposed agreement.

The California State University system responded with a federal lawsuit challenging the investigation and the administration's attempt to impose sanctions over past conduct.

A subsequent court arrangement established protections against immediate disruption of federal funding while providing a process for expedited litigation if the administration moves to withhold funds.

That dispute remains a separate legal issue from the allegations against Kress.

item.title: Biden memoir draws fire for ‘denial’ as critics flag Gaza, racial-equity omissions
item.description: Joe Biden's memoir "Promise Me, America" draws sharp reviews; critics say he stays "stubbornly in denial" about his age, Gaza, and his 2024 reelection bid.
item.content:encoded:
Former President Joe Biden’s new memoir has drawn sharp criticism and opened a debate about how Biden’s choices — and his account of them — will shape his legacy.

Released Nov. 17, "Promise Me, America" defends Biden’s presidency and his decision to seek re-election in 2024. The memoir drew a sharp verdict from The New Yorker writer Amy Davidson Sorkin, who said Biden remains "stubbornly in denial," while other critics scrutinized the book's account of Gaza and what it left out about racial equity. Sorkin’s criticism centers on Biden’s response to questions about his age and his continued insistence that he could have won.

"The true test of a book like this is whether its author will own his losses, too. Biden, for his part, does not," added New York Times nonfiction critic Jennifer Szalai. "He is so preoccupied with burnishing his legacy that he gets awkward and defensive when addressing the two issues many readers will be most curious about: his handling of the war in Gaza, and his decision to run for a second term."

"The news of the memoir, in short, is that there is no real news: Biden is as stubbornly in denial as ever, " Sorkin wrote.

BIDEN ADDRESSES INFAMOUS 'WE BEAT MEDICARE' DEBATE MOMENT IN NEW MEMOIR

The dispute around Biden's recollection of his tenure centers on two consequential decisions — his choice to seek another term and his administration’s policy toward Israel during the Gaza war.

In its review of the memoir, the Associated Press reported that Biden says he believed he was the best person to defeat President Donald Trump and that the Democratic primaries gave him no warning he was in trouble. Meanwhile, Sorkin and Szalai argued in their reviews that Biden gives too little weight to concerns about his age and fitness when recounting that period, despite acknowledging that his debate performance was poor.

"Biden’s voice gets passive; he portrays himself as the helpless victim of events," Szalai wrote. "He gets similarly defensive when recounting the war in Gaza," she added.

BIDEN ACCUSES PELOSI OF WORKING 'FURIOUSLY' BEHIND SCENES TO DERAIL HIS 2024 CAMPAIGN

Self-described socialist website Jacobin and other reviewers, including Sorkin and Szalai, criticized Biden's accounting of his relationship with Israel and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, arguing he described it in the book as if it were much more adversarial than in actuality.

Szalai wrote that Biden gets "awkward and defensive" when addressing both Gaza and his decision to seek another term, and faulted him for how he described Israeli victims and suffering versus Palestinian victims and suffering. She specifically noted that Biden used names to identify Israeli victims but "no names" for Palestinian victims, while calling his language about Palestinian suffering "passive."

"The only consistent position is inconsistency," Israeli journalist and political commentator Amit Segal said of Biden’s account of Israel policy, calling it "devoid of doctrine or strategy. "

Separately, Semafor politics reporter David Weigel noted that Biden recounts signing 17 executive orders on his first day but does not mention his order establishing a government-wide approach to racial equity that mandated every executive agency to develop a DEI action plan. Weigel wrote that the word "equity" does not appear in the memoir once.

"Biden argues instead that 'every one of my legislative accomplishments had justice baked in,' including 'equal access to vaccines,'" Weigel wrote.

"Gender gets the same treatment," he continued. "Biden, who had called anti-transgender discrimination 'the civil rights issue of our time,' never uses the word 'transgender' in his memoir. He doesn’t mention his Day 1 executive order that banned discrimination on the basis of gender identity."

item.title: Cheese aged in military fortress founded by Napoleon just named best in the world
item.description: Comté Fort des Rousses 24 Months, a raw cow's milk cheese aged for two years in a French fortress, won the 2026 World Cheese Awards in Córdoba, Spain.
item.content:encoded:
A cheese made from raw cow’s milk and aged for two years in a historic military fortress in France just took home the top prize in the 2026 World Cheese Awards, a global competition that judged more than 5,000 cheeses from over 40 countries.

Held in Córdoba, Spain, on Nov. 12, the annual showcase aims to highlight local cheesemaking and food and drink culture, according to the Guild of Fine Food, which organizes the World Cheese Awards.

This year, the judges’ overall winning pick was Fromageries Arnaud's Comté Fort des Rousses 24 Months, which gets its name from the former military fortress Fort des Rousses in eastern France, near the Swiss border.

AMERICA'S BEST PIZZERIAS CROWNED IN NEW RANKINGS AS PIZZA EXPERT GIVES SLICE OF SKEPTICISM

Founded in the early 1800s by Napoleon Bonaparte, who viewed the location as "a strategic military position," according to the historic fort’s website, Fort des Rousses served as a military base and training camp before eventually being turned into aging cellars in 1998.

With 50,000 square meters of vaulted stone cellars, the fortress is one of France’s largest cheese caves, housing nearly 140,000 wheels of Comté, the fort’s website says.

Comté is a cooked and pressed cheese made from unpasteurized cow’s milk traditionally made in the Jura Massif mountain region of France, according to Comté USA.

A young Comté typically smells of butter, dried apricots and caramel.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Meanwhile, a Comté that’s aged for a long time will be more fruity, spicy and nutty, the organization’s website states.

The Comté Fort des Rousses 24 Months was aged by cheese maturer, or affineur, JuraFlore, which has been aging cheeses since 1907.

Their Charles Arnaud cellar in Fort des Rousses, which produced this year’s world champion, is dedicated solely to Comté cheeses, according to the website.

"What I liked about this cheese was the complexity," said finalist judge Rafa Dominguez Gonzalez. 

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Those beautiful, nutty, savory flavors really left a mark on me," he added.

"Some people argue that time is the fifth ingredient in cheese," said Patrick McGuigan, a cheese author and educator who co-hosted the judging of the finalists.

Judges blindly assessed the cheeses’ appearance, aroma, texture, flavor and mouthfeel, awarding points based on their evaluations, according to the World Cheese Awards website.

The number of points awarded in the initial round of judging determined whether a cheese won a bronze, silver or gold medal.

Once all the cheeses were scored, the judges chose 108 "Super Gold" winners among the gold medal recipients, which then advanced to be judged by a 14-member super jury.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Each judge selected a favorite cheese for the final round of evaluations, which yielded a three-way tie between the winning Comté, Ossau-Iraty from France and Le Gruyère AOP from Switzerland, with each cheese earning 81 points.

Competition organizers broke the tie by subtracting each cheese’s highest and lowest scores, which led the Comté to win the title of World Champion.

The 14 finalists hailed from Spain, Portugal, Italy, France and Switzerland, with cheeses including a pecorino variety from Italy and an aged goat’s milk cheese from Spain, which featured a coating of edible flowers.

Fox News Digital reached out to JuraFlore and the Guild of Fine Food, the organizers of the World Cheese Awards, for comment.

item.title: Deadlocked Florida election decided by coin toss
item.description: Jennifer Lagner won the Atlantic Beach commissioner seat after a coin flip broke a 3,162-vote tie, with Duval County election officials running recounts.
item.content:encoded:
Jennifer Lagner won the election for Atlantic Beach city commissioner in Florida via a coin toss after successive recounts left her tied with her opponent, according to the New York Post.

Lagner and Lisa Herrold each sat at 3,162 votes after Duval County's Supervisor of Elections Jerry Holland initiated both a manual and a machine recount.

The deadlock initiated the unique tiebreaker last week in which each candidate would have the chance to win two of three coin flips.

THREE HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL TEAMS HAVE THEIR PLAYOFF FATES DECIDED BY A MIDNIGHT PARKING LOT COIN TOSS

Under the city's election rules, each candidate had a chance to call the coin's landing. Herrold went first, calling heads, but the coin landed tails, giving Lagner a 1-0 lead.

Lagner went next, accurately predicting heads to win the contest, securing her election victory to become city commissioner.

"This shows how great and free our country is," Lagner told a local news outlet.

"I am honored to have the opportunity to serve as your next City Commissioner for Seat 4," she wrote on Facebook. "A coin toss was certainly an unexpected and unforgettable way to bring an election to a close! Thank you to Jerry Holland and his entire team for their work throughout this election process."

"Jen and I have been a part of this community for years ... It was meant to be ... We’re going to look back at this and realize how unbelievable this was," Herrold told the local outlet.

SOUTH DAKOTA MAYORAL CANDIDATES SEPARATED BY JUST TWO VOTES IN SHOCKINGLY CLOSE RACE, RECOUNT EXPECTED

Supervisor Holland added, "It’s remarkable, really ... the meaning of that is every vote matters, you know, and one vote can make a difference." 

Last Friday's coin flip wasn't the first time in Duval County history that an election tie was broken in an unconventional manner.

FLORIDA POLLING PLACES IN 7 COUNTIES ARE MOVING LOCATIONS DUE TO FLOODING

In the 2014 Neptune Beach City Council race, Rory Diamond and Richard Arthur broke their tie by choosing from a series of numbered ping pong balls. Arthur, who selected the ping pong ball with a higher number, won.

Lagner, Herrold and the Duval County's Supervisor of Elections did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for further comment.

Reuters contributed to this report.

FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump and UFC President and CEO Dana White will announce six-figure personal contributions to one of America's oldest musical institutions.

The President’s Own United States Marine Band played a key role in America's 250th birthday celebrations and official state business this year — and a White House official tells Fox News Digital that the pair want to "express their appreciation for the band’s exceptional talent, professionalism and commitment to excellence."

Trump and White are scheduled to announce Friday afternoon that they will each donate $100,000 of their own money, which will give each member of the band approximately $1,000. No taxpayer dollars will be used for the $200,000 gift.

The announcement will be made during the first-ever event on the new White House helipad on the South Lawn.

All 135 members of the band will attend alongside senior military leaders, including Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and Commandant of the Marine Corps General Eric Smith.

TRUMP TAPS ‘TRUE WARRIOR’ HUNG CAO AS NAVY SECRETARY AFTER 4 MONTHS AS ACTING LEADER

"‘The President’s Own’ United States Marine Band proudly embodies American excellence and tradition – and their melodies have accompanied defining moments in our nation’s history," White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told Fox News Digital.

"President Trump will partner with Dana White to generously celebrate their elite musical talent and unwavering dedication, conveying his gratitude to some of our Nation’s finest musicians."

The band performed at UFC 250 on the South Lawn of the White House in June, learning each fighter's song in a first-of-its-kind event featuring seven fights.

It also performed at the White House in September when Chinese President Xi Jinping came to Washington for bilateral talks with Trump.

DANA WHITE SAYS 'I DON'T GIVE A S---' IF TRUMP FRIENDSHIP COSTS HIM BUSINESS, 250TH EVENT WAS TRUMP'S IDEA

Band members serve as musical ambassadors for the Marine Corps at national and international venues.

The Marine Band is the oldest continuously active professional musical organization in the United States. It was founded by an act of Congress in 1798 and has served every U.S. president except for George Washington.

Thomas Jefferson gave the band its nickname, "The President's Own." It traveled with Abraham Lincoln to his 1863 Gettysburg address.

For the first time ever, the Marine Band has been nominated for a 2027 Grammy Award. Specifically, the nomination is for Best Orchestral Performance.

There are 10 active Marine Corps Fleet Bands. Members of those bands attend Marine Corps Recruit Training and earn the title United States Marine, and are held to the same standards of discipline, physical fitness and professionalism.

item.title: Republican senator opens door on possibility of a presidential bid, in shift from past position
item.description: Republican Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, who previously said he did not intend to pursue a presidential bid, is now opening the door to the possibility.
item.content:encoded:
Following the GOP’s widespread midterm losses, Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo. — who in September indicated to the Washington Examiner that he had "no intention" of running for president in 2028 — is now leaving the door open to a White House bid.

"After this most recent election, I think everybody that cares about the future of the party, the future of the country, has a lot of thinking to do," the senator said to The Associated Press when asked about his presidential aspirations. "So I’ll just say I have a lot of thinking to do."

JOSH HAWLEY SHOOTS DOWN PROSPECT OF 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID, SAYS HE HAS 'NO INTENTION' OF RUNNING: REPORT

"I was alarmed by the results of the election, and I’m concerned about the direction of both my party and the country," Hawley told NBC News when asked whether he is thinking about running for president. "And I want to do my part there. I’m trying to think through what my part is. But I certainly want to do my part for the future."

"What I said to you is the honest to goodness truth, which is just that I’ve got four years here to serve in the Senate, and I’m just trying to think about where I am and what’s in front of me, what can I do to help the country go forward."

"I'm concerned about what comes next for the party. So I don’t know what my role is in that yet, but I’m trying to give it some serious thought, and I’m no further along than that," he said.

HAWLEY ZEROES IN ON LIA THOMAS LOCKER ROOM CONTROVERSY: 'DID THEY CONSENT?'

Hawley's comments mark a notable reversal, as he previously shot down the idea of pursuing the presidency in 2028, telling the Washington Examiner in September, "No, I have no intention of doing so, period."

item.title: Colombian president calls out 'false' New York Times report on US partnership against narcoterrorism
item.description: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella called a report from The New York Times that says he rejected a joint U.S. operation against narcoterrorism "false."
item.content:encoded:
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella said Wednesday that a New York Times report claiming he rejected a joint military operation with the U.S. to combat narcoterrorism was "false."

The New York Times reported that, according to U.S. officials, de la Espriella said he lacked the votes in Congress to approve working with the Pentagon and the Trump administration, which the publication described as "a major setback for the Trump administration’s campaign against drug gangs." The agreement would have allowed U.S. forces to carry out joint airstrikes and ground operations within Colombia.

The article was published under the headline "Colombia Rejects Joint Plan With U.S. to Target Drug Gangs."

‘WAVE OF FREEDOM’ SWEEPS LATIN AMERICA AS TRUMP ALLY TAKES FIGHT TO MARXIST TERROR GROUP

In an X post, de la Espriella denied rejecting any proposal from the Trump administration, insisting that the two countries maintain "strong and increasingly close cooperation" with each other.

"The information published by The New York Times, claiming that I rejected a plan for cooperation with the United States to conduct joint operations against narcoterrorism, is false," de la Espriella wrote.

De la Espriella added that a request to allow foreign troops into Colombia would fall under the jurisdiction of the country's Congress rather than his office and that he would continue to work with the U.S. to help strengthen Colombian forces.

ECUADOR'S PRESIDENT DENIES US OPERATES MILITARY BASE DESPITE REPORTS OF TROOP BUILDUP

"Any decision will be made in accordance with our Constitution, national sovereignty, and the relevant legal procedures. Our alliance with the United States is stronger than ever, and we have a common enemy: NARCOTERRORISM. Stand firm for the Homeland! Long live Christ the King!" de la Espriella wrote.

The New York Times also reported that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth altered the schedule of his Latin America trip in response to the lack of a deal. In response, Hegseth similarly called out the report for casting doubt on the relationship between the nations.

TRUMP CLEARS HURDLE IN $15 BILLION LAWSUIT AGAINST NEW YORK TIMES

"Amen, Mr. President. The fake news cannot help themselves. Totally false. Our partnership to defeat the narco-terrorists that threaten your country, and ours, is stronger than ever before. The @DeptofWar is with you all the way," Hegseth wrote on X.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, The New York Times pointed to a statement the publication released on X.

"Our reporting confirmed that President Abelardo De La Espriella of Colombia told U.S. officials that his nation would not allow American forces to take part in anti-cartel military operations on its soil. Our reporters reached out multiple times to Mr. De La Espriella’s press team for a response prior to publication, but they chose not to comment," the statement read.

It continued, "After our story ran, Mr. De La Espriella said on X that it was ‘false’ that his government had rejected a cooperation plan. We have updated our story to include his response and stand by the details and sourcing in this story."

Fox News Digital also reached out to the White House for comment.

item.title: Putin launches Ukraine barrage hours after Trump meeting amid alleged Russian missile breach of NATO airspace
item.description: Hours after Vladimir Putin joined Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China, Russia fired more than 400 drones and 110 missiles at Ukraine, killing at least eight.
item.content:encoded:
Just hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin stood alongside President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a historic summit in China, Moscow unleashed one of its largest attacks on Ukraine, killing at least eight people, striking three major bridges in Kyiv and sending suspected Russian missiles and a drone into NATO-member Poland.

The massive overnight assault Friday came as the Trump administration announced progress toward expanding peace negotiations with Russia, exposing the stark contrast between the diplomatic optimism emerging from Thursday's meetings and the escalating war on the ground.

A European intelligence source told Fox News Digital that Putin is preparing an intensified winter military campaign and believes that a combination of sustained battlefield pressure and U.S.-led diplomatic negotiations could eventually force Ukraine to surrender additional territory.

TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE

The source described the photograph of Putin standing alongside Trump and Xi as a long-sought diplomatic achievement for the Russian leader, even as Moscow prepares to increase pressure on Kyiv.

According to the source, Russia's calculation is that Ukraine could be compelled to accept territorial concessions by spring, particularly in the country's east.

"They are very convinced that by spring Ukrainians will give up," the source told Fox News Digital, describing what the source assessed to be Moscow's strategy.

The source also warned that Russian military pressure is increasing despite Ukraine's recent successful strikes against critical Russian infrastructure. "It's going to be a very difficult winter for Ukrainians," the source said.

Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe, told Fox News Digital that the timing of Russia's latest assault should leave little doubt about Putin's intentions, arguing that the Russian leader has repeatedly responded to President Donald Trump's diplomatic overtures with renewed attacks on Ukraine.

"Putin never has been a partner for peace in Ukraine," he said. "And Putin will never be a partner for peace in the future for Ukraine." Breedlove said that Putin's objective is to subjugate Ukraine, install a leadership loyal to Moscow and exploit the country's resources.

RUSSIA PLOTTING 'MASSIVE STRIKE' DURING MIDTERMS, ZELENSKYY WARNS, URGES US TO STOP PUTIN

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, targeting the country's energy, transportation and logistical infrastructure.

The barrage killed six people in Kyiv and two in the western city of Lviv, while more than two dozen others were wounded, according to a Reuters' Nov. 20 report.

Three major bridges spanning the Dnipro River in Kyiv — the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi bridges — were struck, disrupting transportation between the eastern and western sections of the capital.

Russian attacks also damaged railway infrastructure and energy facilities, triggering emergency power outages as temperatures drop ahead of winter.

In Lviv, two people were killed in a strike on the Sknyliv railway station, while additional injuries were reported following attacks on residential buildings and a hospital in other Ukrainian regions.

UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY ON DEFYING US IN ATTACKING RUSSIAN OIL: 'OUR RESPONSE MUST BE PAINFUL'

Zelenskyy accused Moscow of using the attacks to compensate for what he described as military and diplomatic setbacks.

"This was one of the largest attacks," Zelenskyy said in a statement published on Telegram Friday.

Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed carrying out a massive operation, saying it targeted facilities connected to Ukraine's military-industrial complex, including missile and drone production sites and transportation infrastructure.

The competing claims about the targets and the extent of the damage could not be independently verified.

The strikes followed Putin's warning Thursday that Russia would retaliate against Ukraine for repeated attacks on the Kerch Bridge, which connects Russia with the occupied Crimean Peninsula.

Ukrainian forces launched three attacks on the strategic crossing in four days, damaging its road section and disrupting rail traffic.

The bridge, inaugurated by Putin in 2018, serves as both a transportation route and a powerful symbol of Moscow's control over Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014.

UKRAINE STRIKES 'ONE OF THE LARGEST OIL REFINERIES' IN SOUTHERN RUSSIA AHEAD OF PUTIN-TRUMP MEETING IN CHINA

The overnight assault also raised concerns beyond Ukraine's borders after Polish officials reported three separate incursions into the country's airspace.

Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said one of the objects was identified as a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, while another was believed to be a missile and the third likely a jet-powered drone.

Authorities were investigating debris near Nowy Lipowiec, Mołodycz and Rudnik nad Sanem in southeastern Poland.

"There has been a violation of Polish airspace and an incursion by objects from the Russian Federation," Kosiniak-Kamysz said, according to Reuters.

Poland said it would seek additional NATO assistance to secure the alliance's eastern flank.

Breedlove warned that the reported incursions into Polish airspace were part of a broader pattern of Russia testing NATO's resolve. "Mr. Putin will push further and further when there is no cost to him, when NATO doesn't respond, when the United States doesn't respond, in his mind, there is no reason to stop. He will continue," Breedlove told Fox News Digital.

UKRAINE RELEASES VIDEO SHOWING DAMAGE TO PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE FOLLOWING 'UNPRECEDENTED OPERATION' IN CRIMEA

The attacks came less than a day after the Trump administration announced what it described as progress toward a broader diplomatic framework involving Russia, Ukraine and European governments.

During talks in Berlin Thursday, U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said Moscow had agreed to engage in an expanded negotiating format that would include European representatives.

"Russia has agreed to engage in the multilateral format with the Europeans," Kushner said, according to Fox News Digital's Nov. 19 report.

Zelenskyy urged Washington to organize the next round of discussions quickly, insisting that European governments must play a full role in negotiations affecting the continent's security.

But Moscow's position remained less clear Friday, with Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov saying an invitation for European officials to visit Moscow did not mean they had been accepted into the existing U.S.-brokered negotiating format, according to The Associated Press.

The European intelligence source suggested Russia believes the diplomatic process itself could strengthen its negotiating position by allowing Moscow to broaden discussions beyond Ukrainian territory to the future security arrangements of Europe.

According to the source, Moscow is seeking to gain time, maintain military pressure and increasingly focus negotiations on wider European security questions.

The source also described Russian efforts to maintain troop numbers without announcing another large-scale nationwide mobilization.

"They have been able to avoid open mobilization, but they have hidden mobilization," the source said.

According to the source, Russian recruitment efforts include targeting people facing financial difficulties, debt or other social vulnerabilities, alongside continued recruitment from prisons.

RUSSIA'S PUTIN VOWS A RESPONSE 'FAR MORE PAINFUL' AFTER UKRAINE ATTACKS PRIZED BRIDGE IN CRIMEA

The source argued that Moscow is prioritizing manpower over the quality and training of new recruits.

"More quantity, less quality," the source said, warning that inadequately prepared recruits face a greater risk of being killed on the battlefield.

Those recruitment claims have not been independently verified by Fox News Digital.

The source's broader assessment was that Russia believes it can sustain military operations long enough to increase pressure on Ukraine's leadership to accept territorial concessions.

For Kyiv, the latest barrage demonstrated the immediate challenge facing U.S.-led peace efforts: negotiations are advancing while Moscow continues large-scale military operations and Ukraine strikes strategic targets deep inside Russian-held territory.

The events also highlighted the growing risks for NATO as the consequences of Russia's war extend beyond Ukraine's borders.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Senate foreign relations chairman warns of 'horrific trend' as Christians killed in Ethiopia
item.description: The State Department calls for independent investigations after at least 34 people were killed in Ethiopia's Arsi Zone, most said to be Ethiopian Orthodox Christians.
item.content:encoded:
The Republican chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee has warned of an ongoing ‘horrific trend’ of Christians being killed in Africa.

Earlier this month, at least 34 people, the majority said to be Ethiopian Orthodox Christians, were killed in a village in the Arsi Zone, about 250 miles southeast of Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa.

"The attacks on Christians in Ethiopia are a horrific trend," Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, told Fox News Digital in a statement, adding, "The instability and violence in Ethiopia has grave consequences for Ethiopian civilians, the region and American interests."

NIGERIAN PASTOR HIGHLIGHTED BY TRUMP SAYS HE’S NEXT AFTER MILITIA KILLS HIS RELATIVES

Open Doors UK & Ireland told Fox News Digital there has been a string of killings in the area, with some 60 Orthodox Christians killed just two weeks before this attack in November. Open Doors is an international organization supporting persecuted Christians.

A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital they are aware of "reports of killing in Arsi Zone," adding: "Reports of civilian killings in Ethiopia demand action. We call for independent investigations and accountability."

The Addis Standard online news outlet reported gunmen approached St. Mary’s Church in Endeto, Robe District, and at the main entrance shouted "Surrender" before opening fire. Worshipers here are from the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Local security guards, who are said to have fired back to protect community members, are believed to be among the dead.

One resident told the Addis Standard, "If you asked me right now, I have no hope of staying here because I would choose to flee for long-term survival."

The identity of the attackers has not yet been confirmed. An attack last month has been attributed locally to the Oromo Liberation Army, designated in Ethiopia as a terrorist organization.

The State Department, quoting the Ethiopian government’s 2007 census, the most recent available, stated the country’s population is 63% Christian. One local source reports though that three of those who died in this latest attack were Muslim.

SUPER BOWL CHAMP BEN WATSON SPEAKS OUT ON CHRISTIAN NIGERIAN PERSECUTION, DOUBLE-STANDARDS AND TRUMP'S IMPACT

Ethiopia is ranked 36 on Open Doors’ World Watch List of countries where Christians are most persecuted. The organization stated "Open Doors condemns the violence against Orthodox Christians and calls on the Government of Ethiopia to take proactive measures to protect vulnerable civilians from attacks by armed groups operating in the area. Reports from the field point to horrific brutality against Orthodox Christians in parts of the Arsi zone of Oromia."

The statement continued, "We urge the federal government to protect vulnerable communities, including Orthodox Christians, particularly in areas where armed groups are active. We also call on the government to hold perpetrators accountable and help all those affected rebuild their lives."

ANOTHER CHRISTIAN COMMUNITY AT RISK IN AFRICA AS EXTREMISTS AND WAR TAKE THEIR TOLL

Open Doors states the recent attacks in the area started in 2025, when 25 people were killed. 

The attacks have ramped up this year:

In February, attackers stormed a church and a market in East Arsi, killing more than 20 Orthodox Christians and one Muslim guard.

In March, 21 people were reportedly killed in East Arsi Zone.

In May, the 101-year-old Teleta Holy Gabriel Church was destroyed and 50 killed in multiple attacks.

In October, 14 people were killed in Gora Singo and in the Arsi Zone, 46 were killed in multiple attacks. This led to the U.S. Ambassador to Ethiopia Ervin J. Masinga posting, "Such horrific attacks against any group must stop."

In November, at least 34 were killed in Endeto.

Senate Foreign Affairs Chairman Risch added, "It is imperative that Ethiopia find a way to manage its domestic affairs in a way that addresses longstanding grievances and promotes sustained peace."

With fighting continuing in several parts of the country, especially in the border area around Eritrea, the State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "Fighting in several regions of Ethiopia is a concern. We urge all parties to protect civilians and resolve disputes through dialogue."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Ethiopian government, but received no response.

item.title: Hackers use Microsoft Outlook security flaw to steal your login data
item.description: Microsoft Outlook flaw CVE-2026-124194 lets a malicious .msg file expose NTLMv2 authentication data, and Microsoft confirms hackers already exploited it.
item.content:encoded:
You probably know better than to enter your password on a suspicious website. But what if hackers could steal information tied to your Windows login without ever asking for your password? That's the concern behind a Microsoft Outlook security flaw that hackers are already exploiting. Attackers can trick someone into opening a malicious Outlook file that quietly exposes Windows authentication information. That information could help a criminal impersonate you and potentially gain access to systems you use.

Microsoft released a fix on Nov. 10. However, the company confirms hackers were exploiting the vulnerability before the update became available. If you use Outlook for work, this is one security update you should check right away.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

FAKE AI EVENT INVITES TARGET MICROSOFT AND GOOGLE LOGINS

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, involves how Outlook handles specially crafted message files. An attacker can create a malicious Outlook message file, such as one using the .msg format. The hacker then needs to convince someone to open that file in an affected version of Outlook. Once opened, the malicious file can cause Outlook to connect to a server controlled by the attacker. That connection happens without the usual warning about accessing external content. During the connection, Windows can reveal NTLMv2 authentication information. This data helps Windows verify your identity when connecting to certain network services.

The information differs from your actual password. However, hackers may be able to use it in a follow-up attack to impersonate you. For someone using Outlook at work, that could potentially expose company resources their account can access. The outcome depends on the network's security protections and whether the attacker can successfully misuse the authentication information. Here's what makes this especially concerning. The attack doesn't require you to type your password into a fake login page. Opening the malicious file can be enough if your computer can connect to the attacker's network location. Microsoft says simply viewing the message through Outlook's Preview Pane does not trigger this particular vulnerability. Someone must open the malicious file for the attack to work.

Microsoft included the Outlook fix in its November Patch Tuesday security updates. The company's core release addressed 1,093 vulnerabilities, including 63 rated critical. Interestingly, Microsoft classified this particular Outlook vulnerability as moderate, giving it a CVSS severity score of 6.5 out of 10. However, that rating tells only part of the story. Microsoft confirms attackers have already exploited the flaw. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) also added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov. 10. In other words, hackers are already taking advantage of this security weakness. Microsoft has not publicly identified who carried out the attacks or disclosed how many people were affected. The company also hasn't provided detailed information about the incidents. With hackers already exploiting the flaw, it's important to install the security update as soon as possible.

FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN

According to Microsoft's security advisory, the affected products include:

The vulnerability concerns affected desktop Office installations on Windows computers. Microsoft's advisory does not list Outlook.com in a web browser or the Outlook mobile apps as affected products. If your employer manages your Microsoft 365 software, your IT department may handle these updates. However, it's worth confirming that the security fix has been installed. For people who manage their own computers, here's how to check.

The most important thing you can do is update Microsoft Office. However, a few additional precautions can help reduce your exposure to suspicious files and account attacks.

Microsoft has released security updates addressing the vulnerability. You can manually check for updates in supported Windows versions of Office.

If you don't see Update Now, you may need to select Enable Updates first. If the entire Update Options menu is missing, your employer may manage updates centrally. Contact your IT department rather than assuming the software has already been patched. You can also review Microsoft's official Office update instructions.

After installing the update, you can check which version of Office is running on your computer.

For affected volume-licensed installations, Microsoft's November 10 security release includes these updated builds:

These build numbers apply to the specified LTSC editions. They shouldn't be used to check other Office versions. If you're using Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, the correct build depends on your organization's update channel. You can check Microsoft's Office security release notes or contact your IT department to confirm the fix.

Although this vulnerability requires an Office fix, keeping Windows updated remains important.

On Windows 11:

Next, check whether Windows can receive updates for other Microsoft products.

This can help Windows deliver updates for supported Microsoft products. However, some Office installations receive updates through separate services or employer-managed systems. Remember that checking Windows Update alone may not confirm you've installed the specific Outlook fix. Check Office separately. It's also smart to back up important files before installing major operating system updates.

A message file from an unfamiliar sender deserves extra caution, especially if you weren't expecting it. Watch for attachments ending in .msg, a common file format for saved Outlook messages. The format itself is legitimate. However, attackers can abuse it to deliver this exploit. If an email claims you need to open an attached message to review an invoice or urgent workplace request, verify it through another trusted channel. Even attachments appearing to come from coworkers deserve a second look when the request seems unusual.

If something looks suspicious, avoid opening the attachment. Instead, report the message using Outlook's built-in reporting tools when available.

In supported versions of Outlook:

The exact menu location depends on your Outlook version and your employer's settings. If you're using a work account and don't see a reporting option, contact your IT department. Avoid forwarding the suspicious attachment to other coworkers.

Strong antivirus software can help identify suspicious attachments and malicious activity before they cause further damage. Look for protection that includes real-time scanning and behavior-based detection. These features may help catch threats that traditional virus signatures miss. However, antivirus software cannot replace Microsoft's security patch. Installing the Outlook update remains essential for closing this particular vulnerability. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Multifactor authentication (MFA) adds another layer of account protection by requiring additional verification when you sign in. Enable it on your Microsoft account and other important services whenever available. Keep in mind that MFA may not stop attacks involving stolen Windows authentication information. That's another reason updating Outlook takes priority.

If you recently opened an unexpected Outlook message attachment, don't assume everything is fine because nothing unusual appeared on your screen. Here's what to do next.

One important reminder: Changing your password alone may not address every potential exposure from this vulnerability. If you opened the attachment on a work computer, let your IT team determine whether additional security measures are necessary.

Microsoft's November security release covers far more than Outlook. It also fixes weaknesses that could allow attackers to gain additional privileges or remotely execute malicious code. For those of you using a Windows PC every day, the sheer number of vulnerabilities may sound overwhelming. However, not every flaw carries the same immediate risk. In this case, the Outlook weakness deserves your attention because Microsoft has confirmed active exploitation.

The larger concern is how easily a malicious file can take advantage of trusted software. Outlook is part of everyday communication for countless businesses, and opening saved email messages may seem harmless. This vulnerability shows why keeping Office updated deserves the same attention as updating Windows.

What concerns me about this Outlook flaw is how little someone has to do to put their information at risk. You could receive what looks like a routine work attachment, open it and unknowingly expose information that helps a hacker impersonate you. There's no obvious warning telling you something went wrong. And by the time you realize it, the damage may already be done. I also find it troubling that Microsoft rated this vulnerability moderate even though attackers were already exploiting it. Most people aren't going to spend their day reviewing security ratings, and they shouldn't have to. They need software that protects them and updates that are easy to install. My advice is simple. If you use Outlook on a Windows computer, check for Office updates today. Don't assume your computer has already taken care of it.

Should Microsoft be doing more to prevent a single malicious Outlook file from exposing your login information, or do you think keeping your software updated is enough protection? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: 'I Play Rocky' star Anthony Ippolito packed on weight with 'entire lifestyle shift' to play Sylvester Stallone

item.content:encoded:
Anthony Ippolito's transformation into Sylvester Stallone for "I Play Rocky" didn't happen overnight.

Ippolito, 27, packed on the pounds and overhauled his diet to portray the heavyweight boxer in the Peter Farrelly-directed biopic about the making of the Academy Award-winning film, "Rocky."

The New York native explained how he endured "an entire lifestyle shift" before jumping in front of the camera to film "I Play Rocky," which follows Stallone's pursuit to bring Rocky Balboa to life on the big screen — a movie Stallone not only wrote in a few days as a struggling actor, but also refused to sell to a major studio unless he played the starring role.

"So, because knowing Stallone was playing Rocky, who is a heavyweight boxer in the movie, and he was a huge fan of Steve Reeves growing up," Ippolito explained of his preparation for becoming Rocky Balboa.

SYLVESTER STALLONE CALLS HIMSELF AN 'IDIOT' FOR DOING HIS OWN STUNTS, DETAILS NINE BACK SURGERIES

Reeves was known for enduring multiple full-body workouts per week to not only create, but also maintain his fighting physique, and prior to starring in the '58 Italian classic "Hercules," Reeves was credited with bringing bodybuilding to a global level as Mr. America in 1947, followed by Mr. Universe in 1950.

Ippolito gained more than 30 pounds and spent months weightlifting and training in a boxing gym while also learning Stallone's specific dialect to transform into Rocky Balboa.

"Stallone started weightlifting at a really young age, so he always had some type of physique," Ippolito said.

SYLVESTER STALLONE'S ADVICE TO THOSE WHO ARE STRUGGLING 50 YEARS AFTER 'ROCKY' CHANGED HIS LIFE

Ippolito's transformation completely astounded the Academy Award winner, who admitted that he had "mixed" feelings about the film but was ultimately blown away by his character.

item.title: Trump can finally deliver the immigration bargain Reagan was promised
item.description: Attorney Mehek Cooke argues that Trump can fix Reagan's failed 1986 amnesty bargain by mandating E-Verify and codifying border security before any legal relief expands.
item.content:encoded:
Washington broke immigration and now offers America two politically convenient but false extremes: deport everyone or grant blanket amnesty. This choice prevents us from solving a problem intentionally created by decades of government failure, weak enforcement and an open invitation to abuse our laws.

President Ronald Reagan’s 1986 immigration bargain granted legal status to millions of illegal immigrants, while Washington’s enforcement commitment proved temporary and inadequate. President Donald Trump can reverse that historic imbalance by making enforcement permanent and offering compassion through the rule of law. Trump has opened negotiations with Democrats while keeping blanket amnesty off the table. His approach prioritizes the removal of criminals, including murderers, rapists and drug dealers, while evaluating long-term residents with clean records and American families individually under the law.

Democrats are responding to Trump’s invitation with a nonstarter: The Protect Our Neighbors Act would allow final removal orders to magically expire after 10 years and create a pathway to permanent residency for certain illegal immigrants. Due process has already produced those final orders, yet Democrats would create a perverse incentive for illegal immigrants to evade removal until they reach the 10-year mark and qualify for permanent residency. This is the definition of insanity: rewarding the failure to enforce the law and calling it immigration reform.

WHITE HOUSE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER TRUMP ANGERS BASE BY FLOATING ILLEGAL ALIEN DEAL WITH DEMS

History reveals why this is the wrong starting point. Reagan’s 1986 immigration law granted legal status to nearly 2.7 million people while creating employer sanctions and border funding. However, employers were considered compliant if the I-9 documents appeared genuine. The GAO found that 39% of unauthorized workers identified in five major cities used or were suspected of using fraudulent documents, and investigators often could not establish that the employer had the knowledge required for sanctions.

By the 1990s, a Congressional Research Service analysis found that the unauthorized population exceeded its pre-IRCA level. Border enforcement followed the same pattern because legalization was not conditioned on control. Despite increased funding, the GAO found unfilled positions, reduced agent time on border control and failing equipment that left high-traffic areas vulnerable to illegal entry and drug smuggling and unpatrolled. The blunt truth is that compassion without enforceable security became an open invitation to repeat the crisis.

President Trump holds a unique position of strength as he confronts immigration reform because he first enforced the law. In fiscal year 2026, southwest border apprehensions fell approximately 95% below the Biden-era annual average, and Border Patrol completed its first fiscal year with zero releases into the United States. Trump proved that existing law could secure the border when a president has the will to enforce it. For permanent security, Congress must codify his border policies, mandate nationwide E-Verify, impose serious penalties on employers who knowingly hire and exploit illegal labor and limit future presidents’ ability to unilaterally dismantle these protections.

To prevent another failure, any future immigration agreement must include benchmarks: publicly reported removals, zero Border Patrol releases and a fully operational nationwide employment-verification system maintained for at least one year before legal relief expands. Enforcement must serve as a condition for future relief.

TRUMP'S IMMIGRATION OLIVE BRANCH THREATENS TO OPEN PANDORA'S BOX AS EXPERTS WARN OF FAR-REACHING FALLOUT

Rejecting blanket amnesty does not require treating every illegal immigrant alike. A cartel member and a father who entered illegally 15 years ago, paid taxes, raised American children and has no criminal record present fundamentally different cases. To be clear, neither entered lawfully, and good behavior alone cannot erase that violation, but it should matter when a judge reviews the case. Existing law permits certain illegal immigrants in removal proceedings to seek cancellation of removal after 10 years of continuous presence, good moral character, no disqualifying criminal convictions and proof that removal would cause exceptional and extremely unusual hardship to a U.S. citizen or lawful-permanent-resident spouse, parent or child. An immigration judge retains discretion, and Congress caps most grants at 4,000 annually, proving that individualized relief is not blanket amnesty.

FORMER BORDER PATROL CHIEF RECALLS BIDEN MIGRANT SURGE CHAOS AS TRUMP CRACKDOWN DELIVERS HISTORIC TURNAROUND

Congress should fund additional immigration judges to reduce the case backlog and deliver timely decisions. It should also create a streamlined federal review process, so each judge receives a verified case file containing the evidence necessary to evaluate every legal requirement. The solution is not weaker standards, but faster decisions and consistent enforcement.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Washington failed Reagan by trading permanent legal status for temporary enforcement promises. President Trump can now apply Reagan’s own standard: Trust, but verify. Congress must permanently codify border security to ensure no future president can simply erase it with the stroke of a pen.

President Trump can finally deliver the bargain Reagan deserved: a secure border, case-by-case compassion under the law and permanent protection for the American people.

item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on X Friday, before holding a news conference on the issue, that he will be closing the city's largest jail at Rikers Island — but not until five years after the existing deadline.

"Our administration is closing Rikers Island, once and for all, and building a city where we ask ourseelves what a person needs, not just what they're accused of," Mamdani said in a video where he appears alongside Department of Correction Commissioner Stanley Richards, who said he had also once been an inmate there.

The plan will create four new jails by 2029, built closer to public transit, Richards added.

MAMDANI IN HOT SEAT OVER POST MOURNING DEATH OF INMATE CHARGED WITH CALLOUS CRIME: 'ABSOLUTELY SHAMEFUL'

Existing plans to close Rikers call for it to shut down by next year. Mamdani's plan moves that date to 2032. 

"We know that detaining more New Yorkers does not make us safer," Mamdani told reporters in a news briefing later Friday morning. He cited a dramatic decline in Big Apple murders between the 1990s and present day as evidence — from thousands to under 300 a year.
